strategy.why_this_method: The constant 6 has a factor pair, $-2$ and $-3$, that adds to the middle coefficient $-5$, so the quadratic factors over the integers and the zero product property finishes it in one line.
strategy.alternatives: The quadratic formula always works and gives the same roots; completing the square also works but takes more algebra here.

steps.title: Identify the form and choose a method
steps.explanation: The equation is already in standard form $ax^2+bx+c=0$ with $a=1$. When $a=1$, look for two numbers that multiply to $c$ and add to $b$; if they are integers, factoring is the fastest route.

steps.title: Find two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to -5
steps.explanation: Both numbers must be negative: their product is positive and their sum is negative. Listing the factor pairs of 6 (1 and 6, 2 and 3) finds them quickly.
steps.common_mistake: Choosing $+2$ and $+3$, which multiply to 6 but add to $+5$, not $-5$.

steps.title: Factor the quadratic
steps.explanation: Each number from the last step becomes the constant in one factor. Expanding $(x-2)(x-3)$ gives back $x^2-5x+6$, which is a quick check.

steps.title: Set each factor equal to zero
steps.explanation: A product is zero only when at least one factor is zero, so the single equation splits into two simple ones.
steps.common_mistake: Applying this rule when the right side is not zero, for example $(x-2)(x-3)=4$.

steps.title: Solve each equation
steps.explanation: Add the constant to both sides of each equation. A quadratic has at most two roots, and we found two, so this is the complete solution set.

hints: Look at the constant term and the middle coefficient. Is there a pair of numbers that links them?
Factor: find two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to -5.
